# Bring your own MCP tools into the chat

Register a remote MCP server and the chat calls its tools, with per-tool permissions.

STOCKHOLM, 23 July 2026 – The QA.tech MCP server lets a coding agent use QA.tech. Custom MCP integrations work in the other direction: the QA.tech chat uses the team's own tools.

## How it works

Add a server under Settings → Integrations → Custom MCP Integrations, authenticate with an API key or sign in with OAuth, and the chat agent picks up its tools automatically. Connections can be personal, so each teammate uses their own account, or shared across the whole project.

## Permissions per tool

Each tool can be allowed, denied, or set to require approval before it runs. Read-only tools and write/delete tools are grouped so a team sets them in bulk. From October a custom skill can list the MCP tools it relies on, and those tools only load for someone who has that server connected, so sharing a skill never shares access.

## What teams do with it

Sync test cases from a test management tool, look up records in an internal system, file items in a tracker the chat does not integrate with natively. The chat asks the connected server and does the work in the same conversation as the test run.

## About QA.tech

QA.tech builds autonomous QA agents that test web and mobile apps end to end. The agent learns an app by crawling it, writes and maintains tests, and verifies pull requests before they merge. QA.tech is based in Stockholm, Sweden.

keenable.snippet:
The QA.tech MCP server exposes your test cases, test plans, runs, issues, chat conversations, automations, configs, knowledge base, and agent rules to any AI client that speaks the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io). Once connected, your assistant can answer questions like *“what runs failed today?”* or *“rerun the failed cases from run UkxK”* without you leaving the chat.

## Accessing the MCP
The MCP is available at:
```
https://api.qa.tech/v1/mcp
```
Authentication is handled via OAuth.
- On first connect you sign in to QA.tech and pick an organization (and optionally specific projects).
- You can only access data you have permission to view in that organization, limited to the projects you approved.

Most modern clients have a one-click or one-line install. Clients that support MCP OAuth (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ChatGPT, Linear Agent) only need the URL above. API keys still work for CI and clients that don’t do OAuth yet.
- Claude Code
- Cursor
- Codex
- ChatGPT
- Linear
- Continue (VS Code)

```
claude mcp add --transport http qatech \
'https://api.qa.tech/v1/mcp'
```

|---|---|
| URL | `https://api.qa.tech/v1/mcp` |
| Transport | Streamable HTTP (JSON-RPC 2.0), stateless |
| Methods supported | `initialize`, `tools/list`, `tools/call` |

Why does a naive loop re-reason at all? Because an agent keeps nothing between runs unless something around it does. As QA.tech co-founder and Chief AI Officer Vilhelm von Ehrenheim (fifteen years in machine learning, previously at Klarna) put it in a September talk to the CTO Craft community: an agent forgets everything you told it unless someone has built the memory and context handling around it. Stopping that waste is what a harness does. It models the application once (a crawl builds a persistent map that later runs reuse, instead of rediscovering the UI from scratch), routes complex flows to a heavier agent tier and everything else to a faster one, and confirms results with deterministic checks (network assertions, email and file-download checks, API calls) rather than more token-hungry reasoning. It can also keep the loop inside the tools you already use: through an MCP server, a coding agent like Claude Code starts a run and reads results instead of burning its own context to drive the browser. That's not a flaw in Playwright. It's just the nature of script-based automation. It's precise because it's rigid.

Writing tests:

Every change tested against everything it can break, from $89 a month, with credits spent only when tests run.

STOCKHOLM, 2 November 2026 – QA.tech today made its verification platform available to teams of every size. Engineering teams can start free, connect their app and get their first test results in the same session, then move to a Starter plan at $89 a month that scales with how much they test.

AI coding assistants have multiplied the number of changes a team ships, and far less of that code is read line by line before it goes out. The gap is not writing tests, it is verifying every change against the running product. That has been the hardest part of QA to scale, and until now the teams that could afford it were the ones with dedicated QA capacity. QA.tech's agents close that gap for a five-person team the same way they do for a bank.

## What teams get

- **First results in the first session.** A guided setup takes a team from app URL to a running test. The agent crawls the app, builds a map of its features, and runs an initial test before the repository is even connected.
- **Every pull request verified before it merges.** PR testing is included from the free trial. QA.tech tests each change against the running app and reports back on the PR, for GitHub, GitLab and Azure DevOps.
- **Maintenance is never billed.** Creating, updating and maintaining tests is free on every plan. Credits are spent only when tests run, with spending limits and budget alerts to keep the bill predictable.

you.title: QA.tech MCP: Closing the E2E Testing Loop for AI Coding Agents ...
you.snippet:
QA.tech MCP gives AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex an external QA agent that runs E2E tests before PR review to catch missed bugs and edge cases.
Its approach isn't to have the coding agent write its own tests and then grade itself—instead, it introduces an external QA agent: the coding agent hands over its changes, the QA agent runs end-to-end tests on the real application, finds bugs and edge cases the coding agent missed, and sends the results back for the coding agent to fix. The technical foundation of this product is the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
Its core value lies in decoupling: tool providers only need to maintain a single MCP service to be reused by multiple different AI clients, without having to adapt separately for each host. This is precisely the technical prerequisite that allows QA.tech to embed itself as a "pluggable component" into multiple coding agent workflows.
As "testing" is integrated in the form of an MCP service, more similar specialized agents may emerge in the future: security scanning, performance regression, accessibility checks. Coding agents are responsible for writing, and specialized agents are responsible for verifying—this division-of-labor model is worth continued attention. QA.tech uses MCP to connect coding agents to an external QA agent that automatically runs E2E tests before PR review.
